feedback: If a child thinks all rainforest plants are small and ordinary, show the scale comparison (giant tree vs house; lily vs child) and name the giants.
If a child says flowers only grow in the ground, return to the branch close-up: the orchid perches high on a tree branch, not in soil.
If a child thinks the vine is just a rope or part of the tree, point out the liana is its own plant, rooted in the ground, that climbs the tree to reach the light above the shady floor.
If a child says the big leaf is just decoration, show the rain funnelling off its pointed tip and connect shape to shedding heavy rain.
If a child assumes plants look the same everywhere, place several of the rainforest plants side by side so they feel how many different forms live in one forest.
Praise a correct name plus one described feature (e.g. 'the orchid is a flower that grows on a branch') rather than just naming.
activities.intendedInsight: Rainforest plants aren't all ordinary and small — they come in an extraordinary variety, many are giants, and some grow in surprising places and shapes for a wet, crowded, shady forest.
learnerActions: Look at real photographs of a kapok tree, Brazil nut tree, liana, orchid, giant water lily, and a drip-tip leaf.
For the kapok, compare it to a scale reference such as a child-sized figure or a house to feel 'taller than a house'.
For the liana, trace how the rope-like vine spirals up a trunk toward the light.
For the orchid, look at a branch close-up showing the flower growing ON the tree, not in soil.
For the giant water lily, see a pad big enough to hold a small child floating on water.
For the drip-tip leaf, watch or imagine a stream of rain tipping neatly off the pointed tip.
Give each plant a one-line hook and say it aloud: kapok = giant tree; liana = climbing rope; orchid = flower that lives on a branch; giant lily = big enough to sit a child; drip-leaf = funnels rain.
Name at least two rainforest plants, then describe one of them (a giant tree, a climbing vine, or a flower on a branch).
activities.title: Rainforest plant gallery: variety and giant scale

feedback: If the child says 'yes, it takes food from the tree', gently correct: the orchid only perches for light and makes its own food; it doesn't feed on the tree.
If the child can't give a reason for growing high, link it to reaching sunlight above the dark floor.

A full answer names several plants, explains the orchid perches only to reach light and makes its own food, and links tall/climbing growth to competing for sunlight. A partial answer knows some plants and that they grow tall but still thinks the orchid feeds off the tree or can't say why it's high up.
Reward reasons, not just yes/no: the 'why' is what shows real understanding.
activities.intendedInsight: A perching orchid isn't a thief: it grows high only to reach sunlight and makes its own food from sunlight, taking water from air and rain — not from the tree. Tall and climbing growth is about competing for light above the shady floor.
learnerActions: Respond to: 'An orchid grows high up on the branch of a big rainforest tree, not in the ground. Is the orchid stealing food from the tree like a thief? Say yes or no, and then say WHY it grows up there.'
Match each plant to a feature (giant tree, climbing vine, flower on a branch, rain-funnelling leaf) after browsing the gallery.

Discuss follow-ups: Where does a plant get its food — the soil, or something else? Why would it be hard for a small plant to live on the dark forest floor? What is a liana, and how does it reach the top of the forest?
activities.title: Check and discuss: the orchid on the branch
